items.followUp: Define mass and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Awards the mark for the definition of mass.
rubric.how: State what mass measures or represents in a body.

rubric.why: Awards the mark for defining weight as a force.
rubric.how: State that weight is the gravitational force acting on a body; the relation W = mg may also be given.

modelAnswer: Mass is the amount of matter in a body and is a measure of its inertia.
Weight is the gravitational force acting on a body; W = mg.

items.followUp: What would become difficult if friction between your shoes and the ground were greatly reduced? Give one other effect of friction.

rubric.why: Shows an important consequence of losing friction.
rubric.description: Explains that walking or gripping surfaces would be difficult.
rubric.how: Give a consequence involving the loss of grip between surfaces.

rubric.why: Gives another valid consequence of the disappearance of friction.
rubric.description: States another effect of having no friction.
rubric.how: Mention an effect such as difficulty stopping vehicles, writing, or holding objects.

modelAnswer: Without friction between our shoes and the ground, we would not be able to walk because our feet would have no grip.
Vehicles would be difficult to start, stop or turn, and moving objects would not slow down due to friction.

items.followUp: Describe how two masses connected over a pulley form an Atwood machine.

rubric.why: Identifies the essential arrangement of an Atwood machine.
rubric.how: Name two masses connected by a string passing over a pulley.

rubric.why: Recognizes the purpose or use of the machine.
rubric.description: States what the Atwood machine is used to study or demonstrate.
rubric.how: Mention the motion or acceleration of the connected masses.

modelAnswer: An Atwood machine consists of two masses connected by a light string passing over a smooth pulley.
It is used to study the motion and acceleration of the masses.

items.followUp: State the two conditions for a body to be in complete equilibrium.

rubric.why: States the condition for translational equilibrium.
rubric.description: Gives the force condition for equilibrium.
rubric.how: State that the resultant (net) force on the body is zero.

rubric.why: States the condition for rotational equilibrium and supplies the second part of the definition.
rubric.description: Gives the rotational condition and an example.
rubric.how: State that the resultant torque is zero and give a suitable example, such as a book resting on a table.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant torque acting on it are both zero.
For example, a book resting on a table is in equilibrium.

items.followUp: A force of 20 N acts at 30° to the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components.

rubric.why: Shows the method of resolving a force into components.
rubric.description: Explains the geometrical method of resolution.
rubric.how: Describe representing the force as the resultant of components along two perpendicular directions.

rubric.why: Gives the component relations for a force at angle θ to the horizontal.
rubric.how: Write the horizontal and vertical components as F cos θ and F sin θ, respectively.

modelAnswer: Draw two perpendicular axes and represent the force as the resultant of components along these axes.
If the force F makes an angle θ with the horizontal, its horizontal component is Fx = F cos θ and its vertical component is Fy = F sin θ.

items.followUp: What is a couple? Give one example of its action.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining forces of a couple.
rubric.how: State that it consists of equal, opposite, parallel forces acting along different lines.

rubric.why: Shows the effect or a practical example of a couple.
rubric.description: States its effect and gives an example.
rubric.how: Mention that a couple produces rotation, with a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action are different.
It produces a turning effect; for example, turning a steering wheel applies a couple.

items.followUp: Write the formula for the orbital speed of a satellite and state what each quantity depends on.

rubric.why: Identifies the central body's mass as a factor affecting orbital speed.
rubric.description: Names the mass on which orbital speed depends.
rubric.how: State that the speed depends on the mass of the planet or central body.

rubric.why: Identifies orbital radius as the other factor and may support it with the formula.
rubric.description: Names the orbital distance and gives the relation.
rubric.how: State that speed depends on distance from the planet's centre; the relation is v = √(GM/r).

modelAnswer: The orbital speed of a satellite depends on the mass M of the planet and the orbital radius r, measured from the planet’s centre.
Its relation is v = √(GM/r), where G is the universal gravitational constant.

items.followUp: Explain how a solar cell converts sunlight into electrical energy and how solar cells are used in a solar panel.

rubric.why: Describes the function of a solar cell.
rubric.description: Explains what a solar cell does.
rubric.how: State that a solar cell converts sunlight or light energy directly into electrical energy.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a solar panel from an individual cell.
rubric.description: Explains what a solar panel is made of.
rubric.how: State that a panel consists of a number of solar cells connected together.

modelAnswer: A solar cell converts sunlight directly into electrical energy.
A solar panel is made by connecting a number of solar cells together to provide useful electrical output.
